title: Statistics literacy
note: A p-value asks how surprising the data would be if there were no real effect; it is not the chance the effect is real. Confidence intervals show the plausible range, and effect sizes show how big an effect is. Always ask for absolute risk, not just relative risk.

read.title: Reading a health headline
text: A headline announces that a new drug cuts heart attack risk in half. The underlying trial found that 2% of people on placebo had a heart attack over five years, compared with 1% of people on the drug. The relative risk reduction is indeed 50%, but the absolute risk reduction is only 1 percentage point. Put another way, about 100 people would need to take the drug for five years for one of them to avoid a heart attack. That is the number needed to treat.

Neither number is false, but they tell different stories. Relative risk tells you the proportional change; absolute risk tells you how much difference it makes to a typical person. Good reporting gives both.

Next, look at the uncertainty. Suppose the paper reports a risk ratio of 0.50 with a 95% confidence interval from 0.30 to 0.85. The interval excludes 1, so the reduction is statistically significant, and it shows the true effect could plausibly be modest or large.
Finally, remember what a small p-value means: the data would be surprising if the drug did nothing. It does not tell you the effect is big, that it will replicate, or that it outweighs side effects.

q.q: In the trial, what was the absolute risk reduction?
Why is the reduction called statistically significant?
What does a small p-value NOT tell you, according to the reading?
o: That the data would be surprising if the drug did nothing
That the effect is big or outweighs side effects
